profile.summary: Haggai is a brief but decisive prophecy addressed to the Jewish community that had returned from Babylonian exile and still lived in Jerusalem under Persian rule. Although the people were already installed in comfortable homes, the temple remained in ruins for almost twenty years. The book shows the prophet confronting this contradiction: the neglect of the house of God, the material and spiritual sterility of the community and the urgent need to resume the work. Their messages call the people to repentance, the rebuilding of the temple, to the holiness and the confidence that the Lord continued with them. The prophecy also renews hope in the promises of restoration and reaffirms the importance of the Davidic lineage, culminating in Zorobabel as a sign of the continuity of God's plan.
profile.setting: Post-exile context in Judah, after the return authorized by Cyrus, King of Persia, in 538 BC. The initial reconstruction of the altar and temple was interrupted by local opposition and discouragement, leaving Jerusalem in a state of ruin for about twenty years. Haggai utters his messages in 520 BC, in the second year of Darius I, amid severe drought, agricultural crisis, community discouragement and weak political stability under the Persian empire. The book is litsierly composed as a series of short and dated oracles, with rhetorical questions, repetitions and prophetic formulas characteristic. The authorship is not explicitly stated; it is likely that Haggai himself has registered or summarized his sermões.

structure.label: First message: inverted priorities
structure.description: The prophet confronts the people by seeking personal comfort while the house of the Lord remains abandoned; the rebuilding of the temple is presented as the urgent duty of the community.

structure.label: Second to fourth messages: encouragement, purity and davidic hope
structure.description: In the rest of the book, Haggai assures the presence and faithfulness of God, calls the people to holiness according to the law, and to end by reaffirming the importance of David's lineage through Zorobabel.

themes: The centrality of true worship and honor due to God
Practical repentance and resumption of obedience
Holiness of the People before the Lord
Constant presence of God with his people
Hope of restoration and continuity of the Davidic promise
readingKeys: Notice how spiritual discouragement and material crisis appear linked to the neglect of the temple.
Realize the changes of focus between the messages: work, encouragement, purity and davidic leadership.
Note the repetition of prophetic formulas and the emphasis on the presence of God, which supports the response of the people.
profile.cautions: The introduction informs that authorship is not explicitly declared, although it is likely that Haggai has registered his own oracles. The date is relatively precise within the biblical and historical text, but it depends on the post-exile framing and Persian chronology. Reading should avoid treating the book only as a moral exhortation on productivity; its main emphasis is the restoration of the worship, covenant and hope of God's people.

dossier.narratedEra: Post-exile period in Judah/Jerusalem, shortly after the return of Babylonian exile, with the still ruined temple and the Jewish community living under Persian rule. The prophetic action narrated in Ageu is located in 520 BC, in the second year of Darius I, with the resumption of the works of the temple and the joint action with Zechariah. The background includes Cyrus' decree, the initial return of exiles, local opposition, agricultural poverty, and the condition of Judah as a vassal state of Persia.
dossier.compositionEra: The sources suggest that the book was composed between the messages of 520 BC and the conclusion of the temple in 515 BC; the traditional authorship attributes the sermons to the Ageu himself, although the book is silent about authorship. Matthew Henry further notes that the dating of Haggai and Zechariah occurs after the return of captivity, and that recorded prophetic activity concentrates in a few months of 520 BC.

politics.title: Persian Empire and the reign of Darius I
politics.detail: Haggai acts in the second year of Darius I, king of Persia, in the early phase of the Persian empire. The messages are explicitly dated to that reign, and the Jewish community lives under this imperial order.
politics.readingImpact: The restoration of the temple does not happen in political independence, but under Persian sovereignty; this gives weight to the prophetic courage and the promise that God acts even in the context of foreign domination.

politics.title: Cyrus and the Return Decree
politics.detail: The notes place the initial return in Cyrus' decree in 538 BC, allowing deported peoples to return to their lands. The return of the Jews and the beginning of the works of the altar and the temple derive from this authorization.
politics.readingImpact: Upon reading Haggai, the reader sees that the ruined temple is not a failure of divine permission, but of community priority after a promising start that was abandoned.

politics.title: Zerubbabel as the Persian governor of Judah
politics.detail: Zorobabel appears as governor appointed by the Persians, leader of one of the return feats and central political figure in the book. The notes also present him as a descendant of David and, in Ag 2, as the target of the promise of the ring-sineth.
politics.readingImpact: The final message gains political scope: the restoration of the people includes Davidic leadership under Persian administration, which reinforces the tension between imperial authority and Messianic promise.

politics.title: Hostility of local people
politics.detail: The notes mention local pagan residents who threatened the Israelites and discouraged the work, contributing to the abandonment of the flowerbed for nearly twenty years.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read the delay not only as internal apathy, but also as external pressure; the resumption of the work is therefore an act of fidelity under opposition.

politics.title: The importance of David's dynasty in restoration
politics.detail: The final message of Haggai is interpreted as reopening the prominence of David's descendants in Israel's religious and political life. Matthew Henry emphasizes that Haggai and Zechariah prophesy of Christ, and Tyndale links Zorobabel to the Davidic king and the future Messiah.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of the book ends not only with cultual reform, but with dynastic hope: the restored temple points to the continuity of the promises made to the house of David.

customs.title: Comfortable houses contrasting with the temple in ruins
customs.detail: The introduction highlights that the people of Judah lived in comfortable homes, including "forned/ornamented houses," while the house of God remained in ruins.
customs.readingImpact: The material contrast becomes moral argument: the central problem of Ageu is the reversal of priorities between private comfort and public cult.

customs.title: Agricultural economy hit by drought, plague and scarcity
customs.detail: The notes describe severe drought, reduced harvests, pests and widespread poverty. The people worked, ate, drank and dressed, but the result seemed empty, like a pouch pierced.
customs.readingImpact: Haggai does not separate spirituality and economics: agricultural collapse is interpreted as divine discipline linked to temple neglect.

customs.title: Community work for rebuilding and obtaining materials
customs.detail: Zorobabel, Jesua and the remnant resume the reconstruction. The text mentions going up to the hills to fetch wood; the notes observe that the local wood was insufficient and that materials could come from the north, from regions such as Lebanon and Syria.
customs.readingImpact: The cult required concrete logistics and collective work; obedience is not abstract, but involves physical effort and economic reorganization.

customs.title: Cult, altar and temple as the center of community life
customs.detail: The notes recall that, after the return, the altar was rebuilt and the second temple began to be erected; Haggai insists that the proper sanctuary is necessary for worship according to the law.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the temple is not only a building, but a condition for the liturgical life and for the restoration of the identity of the remnant.

customs.title: Festival of Tabernacles as a liturgical context
customs.detail: The second message is dated on the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, celebration of the summer harvest. The notes also recall that Solomon's temple was dedicated at this festival.
customs.readingImpact: The choice of date intensifies the tone of hope: amid the harvest and memory of the first temple, God promises future glory to the new temple.

customs.title: Ritual Purity, Mooring and Feeding Sacrifices
customs.detail: The third message revolves around purity and ritual contamination. The notes speak of sacrificed flesh, clothing that can transmit holiness in a limited way, and impurity transmitted easily by contact with corpse.
customs.readingImpact: The section prevents a purely administrative reading of the reconstruction: without holiness, neither work nor worship produce the quality required by God.

language.title: Rhetoric questions as a prophetic resource
language.detail: Ageu uses rhetorical questions to produce agreement and remove excuses, especially at 1:4 and 2:3, 19. The notes highlight that no response is expected, but adherence to the divine diagnosis.
language.readingImpact: The tone of the book is of pastoral confrontation, not open debate; the prophet leads the reader to self-awareness and confession.

language.title: Oracular Formulas and Divine Authority
language.detail: The notes observe recurring formulas such as the date formulas, that of the message (the Lord said/he sent the word), that of divine discourse (the Lord) and that of covenant (I am with you).
language.readingImpact: These formulas reinforce that Haggai does not speak on his own; the liturgical repetition gives the book the rhythm of authorized oracles.

language.title: "Post the heart" as an invitation to moral reflection
language.detail: The expression is explained as a call to intellectual, emotional and volitional attention, that is, to put the heart on the facts to draw correct conclusions.
language.readingImpact: The reader is led to interpret his circumstance in the light of the covenant, and not only for economic causality.

language.title: Word game between "ruins" and "sequidão"
language.detail: The notes point to a Hebrew pun between the term linked to "ruins" and the term to "dry," bringing the temple condition closer to the condition of the earth.
language.readingImpact: The literary effect symbolically unites the temple and the countryside: the cultual desolation and the agricultural desolation mirror.

language.title: The Lord of Armies as an expression of invincible power
language.detail: The formula is presented as a favorite of Haggai and Zechariah, underlining God's ability to mobilize heavenly armies to act.
language.readingImpact: In the context of political and material weakness, the expression reorients the confidence of the people to the sovereign power of God.

language.title: "Cut a word" and the language of alliance
language.detail: In 2:5, the note observes a unique formulation: "the word I have cut with you," linked to the language of "cutting covenant."
language.readingImpact: This reinforces the continuity between Exodus and post-exile: the same covenant relationship that sustained the people in the past remain active now.

timeline.title: 538 BC: decree of Cyrus for return
timeline.detail: Cyrus, king of Persia, emits decree allowing the return of deportees to their homeland. Notes place this act as the beginning of the post-exile restoration period.
timeline.readingImpact: Haggai is born within a history of previous imperial liberation; the absence of fullness does not invalidate the promise, but shows its incompleteness.

timeline.title: Initial return and interrupted start of the work
timeline.detail: The first returned, led by Sesbazar, begin to rebuild the altar and temple, but the local opposition interrupts and discourages the work, which is neglected for almost twenty years.
timeline.readingImpact: The ruined temple is not a new project, but an abandoned old work; this intensifies the urgency of the call of Haggai.

timeline.title: 520 BC: beginning of the ministry of Haggai
timeline.detail: He preached between August and December 520 BC, in the second year of Darius I. Matthew Henry says his recorded prophecies focus on four months of that year.
timeline.readingImpact: Chronological precision strengthens the reading of the book as concrete historical intervention, not as a vague reflection on restoration.

timeline.title: Immediate reaction of the people to the first message
timeline.detail: After the first message, the people fear the Lord and the work is resumed; the notes say that the Lord has moved the spirit of leadership and the people.
timeline.readingImpact: Obedience is not only human; restoration begins when the people respond and God enables them to act.

timeline.title: October 520 BC and the Feast of Tabernacles
timeline.detail: The second message is dated on the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, the occasion of summer harvest and memory of the salomonic temple.
timeline.readingImpact: The date connects present scarcity and memory of past glory, offering liturgical comfort in the midst of frustration.

timeline.title: December 520 BC: final call to reflection and promise of blessing
timeline.detail: The third message is dated in December 520 BC and the fourth follows in the same range; some notes suggest that from today can refer to the practical start of cleaning the site and preparation of materials, but this is presented as a possibility.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader sees a rapid progression: purification, reorientation and promise of immediate blessing even before the total completion of the temple.

timeline.title: 515 BC: Temple conclusion
timeline.detail: The work is completed in March 515 BC, according to Tyndale's introduction. The prophecy, however, does not mention this closure, which suggests previous writing or near this milestone.
timeline.readingImpact: The message of Haggai belongs to the moment of the resumption, not that of the final celebration; this preserves its tone of urgency and encouragement.

investigation: The traditional authorship is presented as likely, but the book remains silent about the author; Tyndale's introduction assumes that Ageu has written his own sermões, while Matthew Henry only comments on the recorded prophetic activity.

There is a difference between the narrated epoch and the probable composition: the action takes place in 520-515 BC, but the sources do not allow to fix with certainty when the text was written within this interval.
The relationship between Zorobabel and possible political risks before Darius is presented as an interpretive possibility in the note of 2:21, not as a proven fact.
Some 2:18-19 readings on the exact point of the beginning of blessings are debated in the notes; the date may refer to the initial cleansing day of the site or simply to the prophetic present.
The sources are selective: they emphasize temple, purity, david leadership and messianic hope, but do not develop other social aspects of Judah beyond what appears in the notes.

The connections with Christ appear in the introductions and notes, in key confessionaI evangelical; for historical-critical study, this should be read as theological reception of the sources, not as autonomous historical data.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the attached sources and therefore is deliberately selective. No external historical reconstructions, independent etymologies or speculative chronologies were incorporated. Some questions remain open in the notes themselves: the exact date of composition of the book, the historical destiny of Zorobabel, the range of allusions to future imperial shocks at 2:6-7 and the precise sense of certain milestones dated at 2:18. There is also unequal coverage among the sections of the book: the notes detail more the temple, purity and leadership of David than everyday life in a broad sense. References to Christ reflect confessional reading of the sources consulted and should be understood as theological interpretation of these notes.
